paras: The burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule was a pair of night-time attacks in March 1882 on the farm of Isham Edwards, a Black tenant on the Papy place, six miles from Tallahassee, Florida. Unidentified attackers burned about fifty panels of his fence on 11 March and the next night set his mule on fire in its stable, injuring the animal badly. The Weekly Floridian of Tallahassee condemned the attack on the mule as "fiendish cruelty," and the item was reprinted in Savannah.

Edwards rented land on the Papy place, which lay on the Thomasville road six miles from Tallahassee, and the Floridian described him as "a colored tenant." The paper said nothing of any quarrel, accusation or other cause behind the attacks.

On the night of 11 March, about fifty panels of Edwards's fence were burned by people the Floridian called "malicious scoundrels." The following night, according to the same report, "some barbarous villain" entered his stable, fastened bagging to his mule's shoulder, soaked it in kerosene and set it on fire. The mule escaped from the stable, and the paper wrote that had it not, every building on the place and all of Edwards's supplies for raising a crop would have burned. The animal was so badly hurt that the Floridian doubted it would be able to work for weeks, "if ever."
The report named no suspects, and no arrest, charge or later follow-up was found in the coverage.

The Weekly Floridian printed the account on 21 March as a short local item among its city news. Its language was openly sympathetic to Edwards, whom it called "the poor man," and hostile to the unnamed attackers, and it closed by arguing that the heaviest legal penalty, a year in the county jail and a $500 fine, was "light punishment for such fiendish cruelty." It identified Edwards by race but gave no motive for the attacks.

On 29 March the Savannah Morning News reprinted the item word for word in its "Florida Affairs" column, credited to the Tallahassee Floridian, but left out the closing sentence on punishment. No other newspaper coverage of the attacks was found.

reader.title: Burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule
bases: The Floridian reports two night-time fires set on a Black tenant's farm, the burning of his fence and the setting afire of his mule in its stable (A1).
The only report is the Weekly Floridian's local item (A1); the Savannah Morning News printed it word for word with credit to the Floridian (A2), so it adds no independent account.

accounts.label: Tallahassee local item
accounts.gist: Unknown persons burned about fifty panels of Edwards's fence on the night of the 11th; the next night someone set kerosene-soaked bagging afire on his mule in the stable, and the paper said only the animal's escape saved the buildings and his crop supplies.

accounts.label: Savannah reprint
accounts.gist: The same account, credited to the Tallahassee Floridian, in a column of Florida news.

framing.detail: The Floridian called the perpetrators 'malicious scoundrels' and a 'barbarous villain', described Edwards sympathetically as 'the poor man', and called the attack 'fiendish cruelty' deserving more than the legal maximum.
The Savannah Morning News ran the item under its 'Florida Affairs' heading without comment or the penalty sentence.

quotes: Isham Edwards, a colored tenant on the Papy place, six miles from the city, on the Thomasville road, had about fifty panels of fence burned by malicious scoundrels.
some barbarous villain went to his stable, securely fastened a lot of bagging on his mule's shoulder, saturated it with kerosene, and set it on fire.
The severest penalty imposed by our laws-one year in the county jail and a fine of $500-is light punishment for such fiendish cruelty.
